questions.question: Which schedule of the Constitution specifies the division of powers between union and states?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**7th Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **7th Schedule** of the **Constitution of India** provides the framework for the **division of powers** between the **Union Government** and the **State Governments**.
 
• It implements **Article 246** of the Constitution, which deals with the legislative competence of the **Parliament** and the **State Legislatures**.
 
• The schedule is divided into three lists: **List I (Union List)**, **List II (State List)**, and **List III (Concurrent List)**.
 
• The **Union List** currently contains **100 subjects** (originally 97), including critical matters of national importance such as **Defense**, **Foreign Affairs**, **Railways**, and **Currency**.
 
• The **State List** comprises **61 subjects** (originally 66) like **Public Order**, **Police**, **Public Health**, and **Sanitation**, over which states have exclusive jurisdiction.
 
• The **Concurrent List** has **52 subjects** (originally 47) including **Education**, **Forests**, and **Criminal Law**, where both the Union and States can make laws, with the **Union law** prevailing in case of conflict.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **5th Schedule**

 
 
• Contains provisions relating to the administration and control of **Scheduled Areas** and **Scheduled Tribes** in any state except the four North-Eastern states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
 
 
 
• **9th Schedule**
 
 
• Introduced by the **1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951**, to protect land reform laws and other statutes from **judicial review** on the grounds of violation of fundamental rights.
 
 
 
• **10th Schedule**
 
 
• Known as the **Anti-Defection Law**, it was added by the **52nd Amendment Act, 1985**, specifying grounds for disqualification of members of legislative bodies due to defection.

questions.question: The oath of office to the governor is administered by:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chief Justice of High Court**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Every **Governor** and every person discharging the functions of the Governor must make and subscribe to an oath or affirmation before entering their office as per **Article 159** of the **Constitution of India**.
 
• The oath is administered in the presence of the **Chief Justice** of the **High Court** that exercises jurisdiction over that particular State.
 
• In the event that the **Chief Justice** is unavailable or the position is vacant, the **senior-most Judge** of that **High Court** who is currently available performs the duty of administering the oath.
 
• The specific format of the oath requires the Governor to swear to faithfully execute the office and to **preserve, protect, and defend** the Constitution and the law to the best of their ability.
 
• This constitutional requirement ensures that the **Head of the State Executive** is formally bound to the legal framework of the state and the **Union of India** before assuming any official duties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **President of India**

 
 
• According to **Article 155**, the **President** is the authority responsible for the **appointment** of the Governor by warrant under his hand and seal.
 
• The Governor holds office during the **pleasure of the President** as stipulated in **Article 156**.
 
 
 
• **Chief Minister**
 
 
• The **Governor** administers the oath of office and secrecy to the **Chief Minister** and the **Council of Ministers** under **Article 164**.
 
• The Chief Minister serves as the **head of the government** at the state level, whereas the Governor is the **nominal executive head**.
 
 
 
• **Eligibility and Tenure**
 
 
• To be eligible for the post of Governor under **Article 157**, a person must be a **citizen of India** and have completed **35 years of age**.
 
• The normal tenure of a Governor is **five years**, but they can resign earlier by addressing a letter to the **President**.

questions.question: kalbelia dance is a traditional folk dance of which Indian state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajasthan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kalbelia** is a traditional folk dance and music form performed by the nomadic **Kalbelia tribe**, who primarily reside in the **Thar Desert** region of **Rajasthan**.
 
• The dance is often referred to as the **Snake Charmer Dance** because the tribe is historically known for catching snakes and trading snake venom; their dance movements and costumes resemble the slithering of a **Cobra**.
 
• In **2010**, **UNESCO** included the **Kalbelia** folk songs and dances in its **Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity**, recognizing its cultural significance.
 
• The performance is characterized by the use of the **Pungi** (a wind instrument), **Duf**, **Been**, and **Khanjari**, while female dancers perform in flowing black **Angrakha** and **Lehenga** embroidered with silver patterns.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gujarat**:

 
 
• Commonly associated with **Garba** and **Dandiya Raas**, which are circular dances performed during the **Navratri** festival.
 
• **Bhavai** is a popular folk theatre and dance form involving balancing multiple brass pitchers on the head.
 
 
 
• **Punjab**:
 
 
• **Bhangra** is a vigorous folk dance performed by men to celebrate the harvest season and **Baisakhi**.
 
• **Giddha** is a popular female folk dance characterized by rhythmic clapping and traditional **Boliyan** singing.
 
 
 
• **Maharashtra**:
 
 
• **Lavani** is a combination of traditional song and dance performed to the powerful beats of the **Dholki**.
 
• **Koli** is the traditional dance of the **Koli** fishing community, portraying their daily activities of rowing and fishing.

questions.question: Which part of India experiences the highest rainfall due to the monsoon?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mawsynram, Meghalaya**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mawsynram** is a small village located in the **East Khasi Hills** district of **Meghalaya**, positioned at an altitude of approximately **1,400 meters** above sea level.
 
• It is globally recognized as the **wettest place on Earth**, holding the **Guinness World Record** for receiving an average annual rainfall of about **11,872 millimeters**.
 
• The high precipitation is primarily caused by the **Bay of Bengal branch** of the **Southwest Monsoon**, which carries vast amounts of moisture from the sea toward the Indian subcontinent.
 
• The region features a unique **funnel-shaped topography** formed by the **Khasi Hills**, which traps moisture-laden clouds and forces them to rise abruptly.
 
• This forced ascent, known as the **orographic effect**, causes the air to cool rapidly and condense, leading to heavy and persistent rainfall during the monsoon months from **June to September**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cherrapunji (Sohra)**

 
 
• Located just **15 kilometers** from Mawsynram, it was previously the world record holder for rainfall and still holds historical records for the highest rainfall in a single month and year.
 
 
 
• **Kerala Coast**
 
 
• This region marks the **onset of the monsoon** in India, receiving the first rains of the **Arabian Sea branch** around **June 1st**, though its total annual volume is less than the northeastern plateau.
 
 
 
• **Western Rajasthan**
 
 
• This is an **arid region** because the **Aravalli Range** is oriented parallel to the path of the monsoon winds, providing no barrier to force the clouds upward for precipitation.
 
 
 
• **Konkan Coast**
 
 
• Situated on the windward side of the **Western Ghats**, it receives heavy rainfall (over **3,000 mm**), but the coastal barrier is less effective at trapping clouds compared to the Khasi Hills.

questions.question: "Ghare-Baire" (The Home and the World), which critiques the Swadeshi Movement, was written by which Bengali literateur?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rabindranath Tagore**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ghare-Baire**, translated as **The Home and the World**, is a landmark novel published in **1916** by the Nobel laureate **Rabindranath Tagore**.
 
• The narrative is set against the backdrop of the **Swadeshi Movement**, which emerged following the **Partition of Bengal** in **1905** by **Lord Curzon**.
 
• The story explores the conflict between traditionalism and modern radicalism through three main characters: **Bimala** (representing India), **Nikhil** (representing rationalism and global humanism), and **Sandip** (representing fiery, divisive nationalism).
 
• Through **Nikhil**, Tagore critiques the **Swadeshi Movement** for its coercive nature and the potential for communal disharmony, emphasizing that moral principles should not be sacrificed for political ends.
 
• The novel is significant for its **psychological depth** and its use of three distinct first-person perspectives to reflect the internal struggles of its protagonists.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay**:

 
 
• He was an iconic Bengali novelist best known for **Anandamath** (1882), which featured the hymn **Vande Mataram**.
 
• His work largely focused on **historical romances** and the **nationalistic awakening** of India.
 
 
 
• **Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay**:
 
 
• A prolific writer who focused on the **social issues** of rural Bengal and the plight of the marginalized.
 
• Famous works include **Devdas**, **Parineeta**, and **Pather Dabi**, the latter of which was banned by the British government for its revolutionary themes.
 
 
 
• **Bhabani Bhattacharya**:
 
 
• An Indo-Anglian novelist known for works like **So Many Hungers!** (1947), which depicted the **Bengal Famine** of 1943.
 
• His writing often bridged the gap between **social realism** and political commentary.

questions.question: Which young revolutionary assassinated a British magistrate at age 14 during India's freedom struggle?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Suniti Choudhury**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Suniti Choudhury** (1917–1988) was a prominent Indian nationalist who, at the remarkably young age of **14**, participated in a daring revolutionary act against the British Raj.
 
• On **December 14, 1931**, she along with her classmate **Santi Ghose**, assassinated **Charles Geoffrey Buckland Stevens**, who was the **District Magistrate** of **Comilla** (present-day Bangladesh).
 
• The two young girls gained entry into the Magistrate's office under the pretext of presenting a **petition** for a swimming competition among their schoolmates.
 
• During the meeting, they drew **automatic revolvers** hidden under their shawls and fired at Stevens, killing him instantly.
 
• Both girls were members of the **Jugantar** revolutionary group and the **Chhatri Sangha**, an organization for female students dedicated to the cause of Indian independence.
 
• Because of her minor status at the time of the trial, Suniti was sentenced to **life imprisonment** rather than the death penalty; she was released in **1939** during a general amnesty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Matangini Hazra**:

 
 
• Affectionately known as **Gandhi Buri** (Old Lady Gandhi).
 
• She was shot dead by British Indian police in **1942** during the **Quit India Movement** in **Tamluk**, West Bengal, while leading a procession with the Indian National Flag.
 
 
 
• **Aruna Asaf Ali**:
 
 
• Widely known as the **Grand Old Lady** of the independence movement.
 
• She gained fame for hoisting the **Indian National Flag** at the **Gowalia Tank Maidan** in Bombay during the **Quit India Movement** in **1942**.
 
 
 
• **Tara Rani Srivastava**:
 
 
• A dedicated freedom fighter from **Bihar**.
 
• During the **Quit India Movement**, she continued to lead a protest toward the **Siwan police station** even after her husband was shot by the police, demonstrating exceptional bravery.

questions.question: Which city is renowned for its French Quarter, showcasing a blend of French and Indian architectural styles?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pondicherry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pondicherry**, now officially known as **Puducherry**, was the headquarters of **French India** and remained under French administration until **1954**, leaving a lasting impact on its urban design.
 
• The city is uniquely organized into a **grid layout**, a legacy of 18th-century French town planning, and is historically divided into the **French Quarter** (Ville Blanche) and the **Indian Quarter** (Ville Noire).
 
• The **French Quarter** is globally renowned for its **neoclassical architecture**, featuring Mediterranean-style villas with pale yellow or peach stucco walls, arched windows, and **bougainvillea-lined streets**.
 
• The architectural landscape exhibits a specific fusion known as **Franco-Tamil architecture**, where colonial street-facing facades blend with traditional **Tamil features** like large wooden doors and interior courtyards (Thinnai).
 
• Notable landmarks showcasing this hybrid style include the **Raj Niwas** (the Governor's residence), the **French Institute of Pondicherry**, and various Catholic churches like the **Eglise de Notre Dame des Anges**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mumbai**

 
 
• Primarily known for its **Victorian Gothic** and **Art Deco** architecture, exemplified by the **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus** and the Marine Drive cluster.
 
 
 
• **Kolkata**
 
 
• Often called the 'City of Palaces', it is famous for **British Colonial** styles, including the **Victoria Memorial** and **Writers' Building**, reflecting **Palladian** and **Baroque** influences.
 
 
 
• **Chennai**
 
 
• Recognized as a pioneer of the **Indo-Saracenic** style, which blends **Islamic**, **Hindu**, and **Gothic** elements, visible in the **Chepauk Palace** and the **Senate House**.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context**
 
 
• The **Treaty of Cession** was signed between India and France in **1956**, leading to the legal integration of the territory into the **Indian Union** in **1962**.

questions.concept: Origin and evolution of Universe Solar system
questions.question:
The axial tilt of Uranus is about 98°, meaning it rotates almost on its side.

What effect does this have on Uranus' seasons?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Extreme seasonal changes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The axial tilt of **Uranus** is approximately **97.77 degrees** (often rounded to 98 degrees), which means its axis of rotation is nearly parallel to its **orbital plane**.
 
• Because of this unique orientation, **Uranus** rotates essentially on its side, unlike other planets whose axes are more or less perpendicular to their orbits.
 
• This extreme tilt results in the **Sun** shining directly over each pole for a massive portion of the planet's year; since Uranus takes **84 Earth years** to orbit the Sun, each pole experiences **21 years of continuous sunlight** followed by **21 years of total darkness**.
 
• These conditions lead to the most **dramatic seasonal variations** observed in the solar system, where sunlight distribution shifts from being concentrated entirely at one pole to being distributed along the equator during **equinoxes**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Atmospheric Temperature**: Despite the extreme seasonal sunlight, **Uranus** holds the title of the **coldest planet** in the solar system, with minimum temperatures reaching 49 Kelvin (−224 degrees Celsius).
 
• **Rotation Direction**: **Uranus** exhibits **retrograde rotation**, meaning it spins in the opposite direction to its orbital motion, a trait shared only with **Venus**.
 
• **Magnetic Field**: The planet's magnetic field is unusual because it does not originate from the geometric center and is tilted at an angle of **59 degrees** from the axis of rotation, further complicating its **magnetosphere** interactions during different seasons.
 
• **Equinox Dynamics**: During its equinoxes, the planet experiences a rapid **day-night cycle** of about 17 hours, but during **solstices**, the side facing the Sun remains in **permanent daylight** for decades.

questions.question:
The light from a star 100 light years away takes about 100 years to reach Earth.

How long will the star appear to us after it explodes (if it explodes now)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**In 100 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **light-year** is a unit of astronomical distance representing the total distance that **light** travels in a vacuum in one Julian year (approximately 365.25 days).
 
• Light travels at a finite, constant speed of approximately **299,792,458 meters per second** (commonly rounded to **3 × 10⁸ m/s**).
 
• If a celestial object, such as a **star**, is located **100 light-years** away from **Earth**, it means the electromagnetic radiation (light) emitted by that star must traverse a distance that requires exactly **100 years** of travel time.
 
• When a star **explodes**, the visual information and energy from the event begin traveling outward at the **speed of light**; therefore, there is a time lag between the physical event and its **observation** on Earth.
 
• Since the distance is 100 light-years, the light from an explosion occurring **'now'** will not reach an observer's eyes until **100 years** have passed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lookback Time:**

 
 
• In **astronomy**, because light takes time to travel, looking further into space is equivalent to looking further back in **time**.
 
• We never see the universe as it exists at this exact moment, but rather as it was when the light was first **emitted**.
 
 
 
• **Scale of a Light-Year:**
 
 
• One **light-year** is approximately **9.46 trillion kilometers** (9.46 × 10¹² km).
 
• For context, light from the **Sun** takes about **8 minutes and 20 seconds** to reach Earth, meaning we see the Sun as it was over eight minutes ago.
 
 
 
• **Speed of Light Constraint:**
 
 
• According to **Einstein's Theory of Relativity**, nothing can travel faster than the **speed of light (c)**; hence, no signal or information about the explosion can reach Earth **immediately** or in **1 year**.

questions.question: Mary Kom won a bronze medal in boxing at the Olympics in which year and at which venue?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2012, London**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mary Kom**, also known as **Magnificent Mary**, secured the **bronze medal** in the **flyweight (51 kg)** category at the **2012 Summer Olympics** held in **London**.
 
• The **2012 London Games** marked the historic debut of **women boxing** in the Olympic program, where Mary Kom was the sole Indian woman boxer to qualify.
 
• During her Olympic journey, she defeated Karolina Michalczuk and Maroua Rahali before losing to **Nicola Adams** of Great Britain in the semi-finals, which earned her the bronze.
 
• With this achievement, she became the first **Indian female boxer** to win an Olympic medal and only the third Indian woman overall to win an Olympic medal after Karnam Malleswari and Saina Nehwal.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Olympic Venues and Mary Kom's Participation:**

 
 
• **2008 Beijing:** Women boxing was not yet an **Olympic sport**; it was officially sanctioned for inclusion by the **International Olympic Committee (IOC)** only in 2009.
 
• **2016 Rio de Janeiro:** Mary Kom failed to qualify for the **Rio Olympics** after she was unable to secure a berth during the **World Boxing Championships** held in Astana.
 
• **2020 Tokyo:** She participated in the **flyweight category** but was eliminated in the **Round of 16** after a split-decision loss to Colombia's Ingrit Valencia.
 
• **Major Achievements:** She is a record **six-time World Amateur Boxing Champion** and the only female boxer to win a medal in each of the first seven World Championships.
 
• **Honors:** She has been conferred with India's highest civilian awards, including the **Padma Vibhushan** (2020), **Padma Bhushan** (2013), and the **Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award** (2009).

questions.question: Bone belongs to which category of animal tissues?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Connective tissue**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Bone is a specialized form of **skeletal connective tissue** that constitutes the majority of the **endoskeleton** in vertebrates, providing structural support and shape.
 
• It is distinguished by a hard, non-pliable **extracellular matrix** that is heavily impregnated with **calcium salts** (primarily hydroxyapatite) and **collagen fibers**, which provide both compressive strength and tensile flexibility.
 
• The cellular components of bone are called **osteocytes**, which reside in small spaces known as **lacunae** within the calcified matrix.
 
• In long bones, the tissue is organized into **osteons** or **Haversian systems**, consisting of concentric layers of matrix called **lamellae** surrounding a central canal that contains **blood vessels** and **nerve fibers**.
 
• Functionally, bones protect delicate organs (like the brain and heart), facilitate **locomotion** by acting as levers for muscles, and serve as a site for **hematopoiesis** (blood cell formation) within the **bone marrow**.
 
• Bones also function as a metabolic reservoir for minerals, regulating the systemic balance of **calcium** and **phosphorus** in the blood.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Epithelial tissue**

 
 
• Forms the continuous protective layer on the body surface and the lining of internal organs and **glands**.
 
• Cells are tightly packed with minimal **intercellular matrix** and rest on a **basement membrane**.
 
 
 
• **Muscular tissue**
 
 
• Specialized for contraction and movement through the interaction of **actin** and **myosin** proteins.
 
• Includes **skeletal muscle** (striated and voluntary), **smooth muscle** (non-striated and involuntary), and **cardiac muscle**.
 
 
 
• **Nervous tissue**
 
 
• Composed of **neurons** (excitable cells) and **neuroglia** (supporting cells) that form the **brain**, spinal cord, and nerves.
 
• Facilitates rapid communication by transmitting electrical impulses throughout the body.
 
 
 
• **Other Specialized Connective Tissues**
 
 
• **Cartilage**: Has a solid but pliable matrix made of **chondroitin salts**; it provides flexibility at joints and in the respiratory tract.
 
• **Blood**: A fluid connective tissue containing **plasma**, **red blood cells**, **white blood cells**, and **platelets**, primarily used for transport.

questions.question: What is the primary function of chloroplasts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Photosynthesis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chloroplasts** are specialized **double-membrane** organelles found primarily in the **mesophyll cells** of plant leaves and in eukaryotic algae.
 
• The primary function is to perform **photosynthesis**, a process where light energy is converted into chemical energy in the form of **glucose**.
 
• They contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**, which is essential for absorbing light energy (photons) from the sun.
 
• The internal structure consists of a fluid matrix called the **stroma** and a system of membrane-bound sacs called **thylakoids**, which are stacked to form **grana**.
 
• Photosynthesis occurs in two stages: the **light-dependent reactions** (taking place in the thylakoid membranes) and the **light-independent reactions** or **Calvin Cycle** (occurring in the stroma).
 
• The overall chemical reaction can be represented as: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mitochondria**:

 
 
• Often termed the **powerhouse of the cell**, they are responsible for **ATP production** through **cellular respiration**, unlike chloroplasts which produce food.
 
 
 
• **Amyloplasts**:
 
 
• These are non-pigmented organelles (**leucoplasts**) dedicated to the **storage of starch** granules in specialized plant tissues like roots and tubers.
 
 
 
• **Ribosomes**:
 
 
• These are the molecular machines responsible for **protein synthesis** by translating messenger RNA into polypeptide chains.
 
 
 
• **Endosymbiotic Theory**:
 
 
• Chloroplasts possess their own circular **DNA** and **70S ribosomes**, suggesting they originated from ancient **cyanobacteria** that entered into a symbiotic relationship with eukaryotic cells.

questions.question: The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site due to:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rich biodiversity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Western Ghats**, also known as the **Sahyadri** range, were inscribed on the **UNESCO World Heritage List** in **2012** specifically under the **natural category** for their immense global importance.
 
• The mountain chain is recognized as one of the world's eight **'hottest hotspots'** of **biological diversity**, housing an exceptionally high level of **endemism** where many species are found nowhere else on Earth.
 
• The site is comprised of **39 individual components**, including **National Parks**, **Wildlife Sanctuaries**, and **Reserve Forests**, spread across the states of **Maharashtra**, **Goa**, **Karnataka**, **Tamil Nadu**, and **Kerala**.
 
• It serves as a critical **climatic regulator** for the Indian subcontinent, influencing the **Indian monsoon** system by intercepting moisture-laden winds from the **Arabian Sea**.
 
• The forest ecosystems within the range represent some of the best examples of the **monsoon system** on the planet and provide a habitat for at least **325 globally threatened** species.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Endemic Flora and Fauna**:

 
 
• The region contains over **5,000 species** of flowering plants, **139 mammal** species, and **508 bird** species.
 
• Approximately **65%** of the **amphibians** and **52%** of the **tree species** found in the Western Ghats are **endemic** to the mountain range.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO Selection Criteria**:
 
 
• The Western Ghats satisfy **Criterion (ix)**, which identifies outstanding examples of ongoing **ecological and biological processes** in evolution.
 
• They also satisfy **Criterion (x)**, which focuses on the most significant natural habitats for **in-situ conservation** of biological diversity.
 
 
 
• **Other Options**:
 
 
• **Cultural Significance** and **Ancient Monuments**: While India has many UNESCO sites for these reasons, such as **Hampi** or the **Ajanta Caves**, the Western Ghats are listed primarily for **natural ecological value**.
 
• **Mineral Resources**: Though the region has significant deposits of **iron**, **manganese**, and **bauxite**, these are not criteria for **UNESCO World Heritage** designation.

questions.question: Who took an active part in organizing the uprising of 1857 against the British in Lucknow?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Begum Hazrat Mahal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Begum Hazrat Mahal**, also known as the **Begum of Awadh**, was the wife of **Nawab Wajid Ali Shah**, the last ruler of **Awadh**.
 
• Following the British annexation of **Awadh** in **1856** and the subsequent exile of the Nawab to **Calcutta**, she emerged as one of the most prominent leaders of the **1857 Revolt**.
 
• She took control of **Lucknow** and proclaimed her young son, **Birjis Qadr**, as the **Wali** (ruler) of **Awadh**, establishing a rebel administration.
 
• Under her leadership, the rebel forces successfully challenged the **British East India Company** and laid siege to the **Lucknow Residency**, showcasing her strategic and organizational skills.
 
• She actively worked with other revolutionaries like **Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah** and successfully mobilized **talukdars** and **sepoys** against colonial rule.
 
• After the British eventually recaptured **Lucknow** in **March 1858**, she refused to accept any British pension and sought asylum in **Nepal**, where she lived until her death in **1879**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nana Saheb**:

 
 
• He was the adopted son of **Peshwa Baji Rao II** and led the **1857 Uprising** from **Kanpur**.
 
• He was supported by loyal lieutenants like **Tatya Tope** and **Azimullah Khan**.
 
 
 
• **Rani Lakshmibai**:
 
 
• Commonly known as **Jhansi ki Rani**, she led the rebellion in **Jhansi** and **Gwalior**.
 
• She fought against the British forces led by **Sir Hugh Rose** after her state was annexed under the **Doctrine of Lapse**.
 
 
 
• **Bahadur Shah Zafar**:
 
 
• He was the last **Mughal Emperor** and was declared the symbolic leader of the revolt in **Delhi**.
 
• Following the suppression of the revolt, he was tried by the British and exiled to **Rangoon** (Burma).

questions.question: When did the British regain control of Delhi from the rebels during the Revolt of 1857?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**September 1857**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Revolt of 1857**, which began in **Meerut** on **May 10, 1857**, saw the rebel sepoys march to **Delhi** and proclaim the aging Mughal Emperor, **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, as the symbolic leader of the rebellion on **May 11, 1857**.
 
• The British recognized that recapturing **Delhi** was of paramount importance to break the spirit of the rebellion, leading to the prolonged **Siege of Delhi** that commenced in **June 1857**.
 
• British forces, reinforcements from the **Punjab**, and loyalist troops established a base on the **Delhi Ridge** to launch their counter-offensive against the rebel-held city.
 
• The final assault on the city walls began in mid-September, with **General John Nicholson** leading the storming parties through the **Kashmere Gate**; although the British were successful, Nicholson was mortally wounded during the street fighting.
 
• After six days of fierce urban warfare and heavy casualties on both sides, the British successfully regained complete control over **Delhi** by **September 20, 1857**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bahadur Shah Zafar**:

 
 
• Following the fall of the city, the Emperor took refuge at **Humayun's Tomb**.
 
• He was captured by **Major William Hodson**, while his sons were executed at the **Khooni Darwaza**.
 
• The Emperor was later tried and exiled to **Rangoon**, marking the formal end of the **Mughal Empire**.
 
 
 
• **Suppression of Other Centers**:
 
 
• **Lucknow**: The city was eventually recaptured by British forces under **Sir Colin Campbell** in **March 1858**.
 
• **Jhansi**: The fortress of Jhansi fell to **Sir Hugh Rose** in **April 1858**, leading to the legendary resistance of **Rani Lakshmibai**.
 
• **Gwalior**: The British regained control of Gwalior in **June 1858**, which effectively ended the major organized military phase of the revolt.

questions.question: As per SIPRI report published in March 2025, countries in Asia and Oceania accounted for _____ of all arms imports in 2020-24.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**33%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI)** released its annual assessment of international arms transfers in **March 2025**, covering the five-year period from **2020 to 2024**.
 
• According to the data, **Asia and Oceania** continued to be the largest importing region for major arms, accounting for **33%** of the total global volume of arms imports.
 
• While the region maintains the highest share globally, this figure represents a decrease from the **37%** share recorded during the **2019−23** period and **41%** in **2015−19**.
 
• The high volume of imports in **Asia and Oceania** is primarily driven by persistent regional tensions, including territorial disputes in the **South China Sea** and security concerns in the **Indo-Pacific** corridor.
 
• Major contributors to this share include **India**, **Pakistan**, **Japan**, **Australia**, and **South Korea**, all of which remain among the worlds top arms importers to modernize their defense capabilities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **SIPRI (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute):**

 
 
• Established in **1966**, it is an independent international institute dedicated to research into conflict, armaments, arms control, and disarmament.
 
• It is headquartered in **Stockholm, Sweden**, and provides data and analysis based on open sources to policymakers and the public.
 
 
 
• **Global Import Trends:**
 
 
• While **Asia and Oceania** lead, the share of **Europe** has seen a significant upward trajectory due to the ongoing conflict in **Ukraine** and the resulting rush for rearmament among **NATO** members.
 
• **India** remains the worlds largest individual arms importer, largely relying on suppliers from **Russia**, **France**, and the **USA**.
 
• The **Middle East** typically accounts for the second-largest share, with **Saudi Arabia** and **Qatar** being prominent buyers.
